newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Deutsche Bank sees NZ warrant mkt growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Deutsche Bank sees NZ warrant mkt growth.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG may issue more New Zealand equity warrants after the successful launch of its Telecom and Fletcher Challenge call warrants this year, the coordinator for the issues said on Wednesday.
Robert Gipslis of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Australia said the warrants market in New Zealand had tremendous growth potential.

Deutsche Bank launched its Telecom call warrant in February, the first in New Zealand for four years, and soon followed it with call warrants in the four Fletcher Challenge stocks -- Paper, Building, Energy and Forests.

"Telecom was a very successful issue. We issued close to five million warrants during the initial offering period and there was clearly demand in the market for further equity warrants," Gipslis said.
"We felt that Fletcher was a stock which was eminently suitable for an issue."

"The early indications here in New Zealand are certainly that it's going to be a very liquid market," Gipslis told Reuters in an interview. "I'd say it's going to be a very, very quick take-up process."
Deutsche Bank's call warrants in New Zealand give their holders the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying share at a predetermined price at any stage during the life of the warrant.
Gipslis said the global move towards passive investment products had increased the need for equity derivatives.

"I think we're seeing a fundamental shift in the marketplace at the moment. With the emergence of the Tenz fund here in New Zealand, you're seeing a move towards passive products as investment vehicles, but at the same time there needs to be a mechanism whereby the retail market can also get some upside, some trading opportunities," he said.
Tenz is a passive fund based on the top 10 stocks.
The launch of the New Zealand warrants follows a blossoming of the warrants market in Australia in the last two years -- 1.6 billion warrants were traded in Australia in 1996.
Gipslis said one of the reasons he was visiting New Zealand was to look at the potential for more issues here.

"The structure we've got allows us to issue further warrants at relatively short notice -- it really depends on what the market tells us," he said, adding that any further warrants would only be issued on top-10 index stocks which enjoyed good liquidity.
For the relatively small price of a warrant -- the Telecom warrant is currently trading at 23 NZ cents -- an investor gains an exposure to movements in the underlying share price.
Furthermore, Gipslis said the change in the warrant price was a lot steeper than the corresponding movement in the underlying share price.
"So you get leverage from a warrant, and that's what creates the trading opportunities for the retail market," he said.
"What makes the warrant market attractive is it's so liquid it's easy to get in and out of, and transaction costs are low."
Gipslis said Deutsche Bank intended to be the leading issuer of warrants in New Zealand.

"We want to maintain being the most significant issuer in the market. It's a position we have in Australia -- almost a billion of our warrants were traded in Australia last year -- and we'd like to see the same in New Zealand," he said.
